{{Short description|Free swinging suspended body}}
[[File:Oscillating pendulum.gif|right|300px|thumb|Animation of a pendulum showing the [[Equations of motion|velocity and acceleration vectors]].]]
{{Dynamics|rotational}}
A '''pendulum''' is a body suspended from a fixed support that freely swings back and forth under the influence of gravity. When a pendulum is displaced sideways from its resting, equilibrium position, it is subject to a restoring force due to gravity that will accelerate it back towards the equilibrium position. When released, the restoring force acting on the pendulum's mass causes it to oscillate about the equilibrium position, swinging it back and forth. The mathematics of [[pendulum]]s are in general quite complicated. Simplifying assumptions can be made, which in the case of a [[#Simple gravity pendulum|simple pendulum]] allow the equations of motion to be solved analytically for small-angle oscillations.

== Simple gravity pendulum ==
A ''simple gravity pendulum''<ref>defined by Christiaan Huygens: {{cite web | last = Huygens | first = Christian | title = Horologium Oscillatorium | website = 17centurymaths | publisher = 17thcenturymaths.com | year = 1673 | url = http://www.17centurymaths.com/contents/huygens/horologiumpart4a.pdf | access-date = 2009-03-01}}, Part 4, Definition 3, translated July 2007 by Ian Bruce</ref> is an idealized mathematical model of a real pendulum.<ref name="Hyperphysics">{{cite web | last = Nave | first = Carl R. | title = Simple pendulum | website = Hyperphysics | publisher = Georgia State Univ. | year = 2006 | url = http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/pend.html | access-date = 2008-12-10}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last = Xue | first = Linwei | title = Pendulum Systems | website = Seeing and Touching Structural Concepts | publisher = Civil Engineering Dept., Univ. of Manchester, UK | year = 2007 | url = http://www.mace.manchester.ac.uk/project/teaching/civil/structuralconcepts/Dynamics/pendulum/pendulum_con.php | access-date = 2008-12-10}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last = Weisstein | first = Eric W. | title = Simple Pendulum | website = Eric Weisstein's world of science | publisher = Wolfram Research | year = 2007 | url = http://scienceworld.wolfram.com/physics/SimplePendulum.html | access-date = 2009-03-09}}</ref> It is a weight (or [[Bob (physics)|bob]]) on the end of a massless cord suspended from a [[wikt:pivot|pivot]], without [[friction]].  Since in the model there is no frictional energy loss, when given an initial displacement it swings back and forth with a constant [[amplitude]].  The model is based on the assumptions:
* The rod or cord is massless, inextensible and always remains under tension.
* The bob is a point mass.
* The motion occurs in [[two dimensions]].
* The motion does not lose energy to external [[friction]] or [[air resistance]].
* The gravitational field is uniform.
* The support is immobile.

The [[differential equation]] which governs the motion of a simple pendulum is
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}+\frac{g}{\ell} \sin\theta=0</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 1}}}}
where {{mvar|g}} is the [[Magnitude (mathematics)|magnitude]] of the [[gravity of Earth|gravitational field]], {{mvar|ℓ}} is the length of the rod or cord, and {{mvar|θ}} is the angle from the vertical to the pendulum.

{{math proof | title = "Force" derivation of ({{EquationNote|Eq. 1}})
| proof = [[File:Pendulum gravity.svg|thumb|'''Figure 1.''' Force diagram of a simple gravity pendulum.|right|300px]]
Consider Figure 1 on the right, which shows the forces acting on a simple pendulum. Note that the path of the pendulum sweeps out an [[arc (geometry)|arc]] of a circle. The angle {{mvar|θ}} is measured in [[radian]]s, and this is crucial for this formula. The blue arrow is the [[gravitational force]] acting on the bob, and the violet arrows are that same force resolved into components parallel and perpendicular to the bob's instantaneous motion. The direction of the bob's instantaneous [[velocity]] always points along the red axis, which is considered the tangential axis because its direction is always tangent to the circle. Consider [[Newton's second law]],
<math display="block">F=ma</math>
where {{mvar|F}} is the sum of forces on the object, {{mvar|m}} is mass, and {{mvar|a}} is the acceleration.  Newton's equation can be applied to the tangential axis only.  This is because only changes in velocity are of concern and the bob is forced to stay in a circular path.  The short violet arrow represents the component of the gravitational force in the tangential axis, and trigonometry can be used to determine its magnitude. Thus,
<math display="block">\begin{align} F &= -mg\sin\theta = ma, \qquad \text{so} \\ a &= -g \sin\theta,\end{align}</math>
where {{mvar|g}} is the acceleration due to gravity near the surface of the earth. The negative sign on the right hand side implies that {{mvar|θ}} and {{mvar|a}} always point in opposite directions. This makes sense because when a pendulum swings further to the left, it is expected to accelerate back toward the right.

This linear acceleration {{mvar|a}} along the red axis can be related to the change in angle {{mvar|θ}} by the arc length formulas; {{mvar|s}} is arc length:
<math display="block">\begin{align} s &= \ell\theta, \\ v &= \frac{ds}{dt} = \ell\frac{d\theta}{dt}, \\ a &= \frac{d^2s}{dt^2} = \ell\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}, \end{align}</math>
thus:
<math display="block">\begin{align} \ell\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} &= -g \sin\theta, \\ \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{g}{\ell} \sin\theta &= 0. \end{align} </math>
}}

{{math proof
| title = "Torque" derivation of ({{EquationNote|Eq. 1}})
| proof =
Equation (1) can be obtained using two definitions for torque.
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} = \frac{d\mathbf{L}}{dt}.</math>

First start by defining the torque on the pendulum bob using the force due to gravity.
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{ \tau } = \mathbf{l} \times \mathbf{F}_\mathrm{g} ,</math>
where {{math|'''l'''}} is the length vector of the pendulum and {{math|'''F'''<sub>g</sub>}} is the force due to gravity.

For now just consider the magnitude of the torque on the pendulum.
<math display="block">|\boldsymbol{\tau}| = -mg\ell\sin\theta,</math>
where {{mvar|m}} is the mass of the pendulum, {{mvar|g}} is the acceleration due to gravity, {{mvar|l}} is the length of the pendulum, and {{mvar|θ}} is the angle between the length vector and the force due to gravity.

Next rewrite the angular momentum.
<math display="block">\mathbf{ L } = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} = m \mathbf{r} \times (\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}) .</math>
Again just consider the magnitude of the angular momentum.
<math display="block"> |\mathbf{L}| = mr^2 \omega = m \ell^2 \frac{d\theta}{dt} .</math>
and its time derivative
<math display="block">\frac {d}{dt}|\mathbf{L}| = m \ell^2 \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} ,</math>

The magnitudes can then be compared using {{math|1='''τ''' = {{sfrac|''d'''''L'''|''dt''}}}}

<math display="block">-mg\ell\sin\theta = m \ell^2 \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} ,</math>
thus:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{g}{\ell} \sin\theta = 0,</math>
which is the same result as obtained through force analysis.
}}

{{math proof
| title = "Energy" derivation of ({{EquationNote|Eq. 1}})
| proof =
[[Image:simple pendulum height.svg|thumb|'''Figure 2.''' Trigonometry of a simple gravity pendulum.|right|300px]]

It can also be obtained via the [[conservation of mechanical energy]] principle: any object falling a vertical distance <math>h</math> would acquire [[kinetic energy]] equal to that which it lost to the fall. In other words, [[gravitational energy|gravitational potential energy]] is converted into kinetic energy. Change in potential energy is given by
<math display="block">\Delta U = mgh.</math>

The change in kinetic energy (body started from rest) is given by
<math display="block">\Delta K = \tfrac12 mv^2.</math>

Since no energy is lost, the gain in one must be equal to the loss in the other
<math display="block">\tfrac12 mv^2=mgh.</math>

The change in velocity for a given change in height can be expressed as
<math display="block">v = \sqrt{2gh}.</math>

Using the arc length formula above, this equation can be rewritten in terms of {{math|{{sfrac|''dθ''|''dt''}}}}:
<math display="block">\begin{align} v = \ell\frac{d\theta}{dt} &= \sqrt{2gh}, \quad \text{so} \\ \frac{d\theta}{dt} &= \frac{\sqrt{2gh}}{\ell}, \end{align}</math>
where {{mvar|h}} is the vertical distance the pendulum fell. Look at Figure 2, which presents the trigonometry of a simple pendulum. If the pendulum starts its swing from some initial angle {{math|''θ''<sub>0</sub>}}, then {{math|''y''<sub>0</sub>}}, the vertical distance from the screw, is given by
<math display="block">y_0 = \ell\cos\theta_0.</math>

Similarly, when {{math|''y''<sub>1</sub>}}, then
<math display="block">y_1 = \ell\cos\theta.</math>

Then {{mvar|h}} is the difference of the two
<math display="block">h = \ell\left(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0\right).</math>

In terms of {{math|{{sfrac|''dθ''|''dt''}}}} gives
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\frac{d\theta}{dt} = \sqrt{\frac{2g} \ell (\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0)}.</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq. 2}}}}

This equation is known as the ''first integral of motion'', it gives the velocity in terms of the location and includes an integration constant related to the initial displacement ({{math|''θ''<sub>0</sub>}}). Next, differentiate by applying the [[chain rule]], with respect to time to get the acceleration
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}\frac{d\theta}{dt} &= \frac{d}{dt}\sqrt{\frac{2g} \ell \left(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0\right)}, \\
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} & = \frac12\frac{-\frac{2g} \ell \sin\theta}{\sqrt{\frac{2g} \ell (\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0)}}\frac{d\theta}{dt} \\
& = \frac12\frac{-\frac{2g}{\ell} \sin\theta}{\sqrt{\frac{2g}{\ell} (\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0)}}\sqrt{\frac{2g}{\ell} (\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0)} = -\frac g \ell \sin\theta, \\
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} &+ \frac{g}{\ell} \sin\theta = 0,
\end{align}</math>

which is the same result as obtained through force analysis.
}}

{{math proof
| title = "Lagrange" derivation of ({{EquationNote|Eq. 1}})
| proof =
[[File:Coordinates of a simple gravity pendulum.png|thumb|right|alt=Coordinates of a simple gravity pendulum.|Coordinates of a simple gravity pendulum.|300px]]

{{EquationNote|Equation 1}} can additionally be obtained through [[Lagrangian Mechanics]]. More specifically, using the [[Euler–Lagrange equations]] (or Lagrange's equations of the second kind) by identifying the Lagrangian of the system (<math>\mathcal{L}</math>), the constraints (<math>q</math>) and solving the following system of equations 

<math display="block">\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q_j}}\right) = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_j}.</math>

If the origin of the [[Cartesian coordinate system]] is defined as the point of suspension (or simply pivot), then the bob is at

<math display="block"> x = \ell\sin{\theta},</math>
<math display="block"> y = -\ell\cos{\theta},</math>

and the velocity of the bob, calculated by differentiating the coordinates with respect to time (using [[Newton's notation|dot notation]] to indicate the time derivatives)

<math display="block"> \dot{x} = \ell\dot{\theta}\cos{\theta},</math>
<math display="block"> \dot{y} = \ell\dot{\theta}\sin{\theta}.</math>

Thus, the Lagrangian is 

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathcal{L} &= E_k - E_p \\
&= \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - m g h \\
&= \frac{1}{2} m (\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2) - m g \ell (1 - \cos{\theta}) \\
&= \frac{1}{2} m \ell^2 \dot{\theta}^2 - m g \ell + m g \ell \cos{\theta}.
\end{align}</math>

The '''Euler-Lagrange equation''' (singular as there is only one constraint, <math>q = \theta</math>) is thus 

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}}\right) &= \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} \\
\frac{d}{dt}(m \ell^2 \dot{\theta}) &= -m g \ell \sin{\theta} \\
m \ell^2 \ddot{\theta} &= -m g \ell \sin{\theta} \\
\ddot{\theta} &= -\frac{g}{\ell}\sin{\theta}. \\
\end{align}</math>

Which can then be rearranged to match {{EquationNote|Equation 1}}, obtained through force analysis.

<math display="block"> \frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2} + \frac{g}{\ell}\sin{\theta} = 0.</math>

Deriving via Lagrangian Mechanics, while excessive with a single pendulum, is useful for more complicated, [[Chaos theory|chaotic systems]], such as a [[double pendulum]].

}}

== Small-angle approximation ==
[[File:Small-angle approximation for sine function.svg|thumb|300px|Small-angle approximation for the sine function: For {{math|''θ'' ≈ 0}}, the approximation {{math|sin ''θ'' ≈ ''θ''}} can be made.]]
The differential equation given above is not easily solved, and there is no solution that can be written in terms of [[elementary function]]s. However, adding a restriction to the size of the oscillation's amplitude gives a form whose solution can be easily obtained. If it is assumed that the angle is much less than 1&nbsp;[[radian]] (often cited as less than 0.1&nbsp;radians, about 6°), or
<math display="block">\theta \ll 1,</math>
then substituting for {{math|sin ''θ''}} into {{EquationNote|Eq. 1}} using the [[small-angle approximation]],
<math display="block">\sin\theta\approx\theta,</math>
yields the equation for a [[harmonic oscillator]],
<math display="block">\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}+\frac{g}{\ell} \theta=0.</math>

The error due to the approximation is of order {{math|''θ''{{isup|3}}}} (from the [[Taylor expansion]] for {{math|sin ''θ''}}).

Let the starting angle be {{math|1=''θ''<sub>0</sub>}}. If it is assumed that the pendulum is released with zero [[angular velocity]], the solution becomes
{{Equation box 1 |indent =: |cellpadding = 5 |border = 2 |border colour = black |background colour = transparent
| equation = <math>\theta(t) = \theta_0\cos\left(\sqrt\frac{g}{\ell}\,t\right) \quad\quad\quad\quad \theta_0 \ll 1.</math>
| title=}}
The motion is [[simple harmonic motion]] where {{math|''θ''<sub>0</sub>}} is the [[amplitude (wave motion)|amplitude]] of the oscillation (that is, the maximum angle between the rod of the pendulum and the vertical). The corresponding approximate [[period (physics)|period]] of the motion is then
{{Equation box 1 |indent =: |cellpadding = 5 |border = 2 |border colour = black |background colour = transparent
| equation = <math>T_0 = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac\ell g} \quad\quad\quad\quad\quad \theta_0 \ll 1</math>
}}
which is known as [[Christiaan Huygens]]'s law for the period. Note that under the small-angle approximation, the period is independent of the amplitude {{math|''θ''<sub>0</sub>}}; this is the property of [[Isochronous|isochronism]] that [[Galileo]] discovered.

== Rule of thumb for pendulum length ==
<math display="block">T_0 = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac \ell g}</math> gives <math display="block"> \ell = \frac{g}{\pi^2}\frac{T_0^2} 4.</math>

If [[International System of Units|SI units]] are used (i.e. measure in metres and seconds), and assuming the measurement is taking place on the Earth's surface, then {{math|''g'' ≈ 9.81 m/s<sup>2</sup>}}, and {{math|{{sfrac|''g''|π<sup>2</sup>}} ≈ 1 m/s<sup>2</sup>}} (0.994 is the approximation to 3 decimal places).

Therefore, relatively reasonable approximations for the length and period are:
<math display="block">\begin{align} \ell &\approx \frac{T_0^2}{4}, \\ T_0 &\approx 2 \sqrt\ell \end{align}</math>
where {{math|''T''<sub>0</sub>}} is the number of seconds between ''two'' beats (one beat for each side of the swing), and {{mvar|l}} is measured in metres.

== Arbitrary-amplitude period ==
[[Image:Pendulum period.svg|thumb|'''Figure 3.''' Deviation of the "true" period of a pendulum from the small-angle approximation of the period. "True" value was obtained numerically evaluating the elliptic integral. |right|300px]]

[[Image:Pendulum rel error.svg|thumb|'''Figure 4.''' Relative errors using the power series for the period.|right|300px]]

[[File:Pendulum phase portrait.svg|thumb|312x312px|'''Figure 5.''' Potential energy and [[phase portrait]] of a simple pendulum. Note that the {{mvar|x}}-axis, being angle, wraps onto itself after every 2{{pi}} radians.]]

For amplitudes beyond the [[small angle approximation]], one can compute the exact period by first inverting the equation for the angular velocity obtained from the energy method ({{EquationNote|Eq. 2}}),
<math display="block">\frac{dt}{d\theta} = \sqrt\frac\ell{2g}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0}}</math>
and then integrating over one complete cycle,
<math display="block">T = t(\theta_0 \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow -\theta_0 \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow\theta_0),</math>
or twice the half-cycle
<math display="block">T = 2 t(\theta_0 \rightarrow 0 \rightarrow -\theta_0),</math>
or four times the quarter-cycle
<math display="block">T = 4 t(\theta_0 \rightarrow 0),</math>
which leads to
<math display="block">T = 4\sqrt\frac\ell{2g}\int^{\theta_0}_0 \frac{d\theta}{\sqrt{\cos\theta-\cos\theta_0}} .</math>

Note that this is an [[improper integral]] because the integrand has singularities at <math>\theta = \pm \theta_0 + 2 \pi \mathbb{Z}</math>, but these singularities are integrable as long as <math>0 < \theta_0 < \pi</math>.  At <math>\theta_0 = \pm \pi</math>, the singularities become non-integrable, implying that the integral's value diverges as the maximum swing angle approaches the vertical
<math display="block"> \lim_{\theta_0 \to \pi} T = \infty, </math>
so that a pendulum with just the right energy to go vertical will never actually get there. (Conversely, a pendulum close to its maximum can take an arbitrarily long time to fall down.)

This integral can be rewritten in terms of [[elliptic integral]]s as
<math display="block">T = 4\sqrt\frac\ell g F\left( \frac{\pi} 2, \sin \frac{\theta_0} 2\right) </math>
where {{mvar|F}} is the [[elliptic integral#Incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind|incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind]] defined by
<math display="block">F(\varphi , k) = \int_0^\varphi \frac {du} {\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2 u}}\,.</math>

Or more concisely by the [[integration by substitution|substitution]]
<math display="block">\sin{u} = \frac{\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}{\sin\frac{\theta_0}{2}}</math>
expressing {{mvar|θ}} in terms of {{mvar|u}},

{{Equation box 1 |indent =: |cellpadding = 5 |border = 2 |border colour = black |background colour = transparent
|equation =<math>T = \frac{2 T_0}{\pi} K(k), \qquad \text{where} \quad k=\sin\frac{\theta_0}{2}.</math>{{pad|2em}}{{EquationRef|Eq. 3}}
}}
Here {{mvar|K}} is the [[elliptic integral#Complete elliptic integral of the first kind|complete elliptic integral of the first kind]] defined by

<math display="block">K(k) = F \left( \frac \pi 2, k \right) = \int_0^\frac{\pi}{2} \frac{du}{\sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2 u}}\,.</math>

For comparison of the approximation to the full solution, consider the period of a pendulum of length 1&nbsp;m on Earth ({{mvar|g}} = {{val|9.80665|u=m/s<sup>2</sup>}}) at an initial angle of 10 degrees is
<math display="block">4\sqrt{\frac{1\text{ m}}{g}}\ K\left(\sin\frac{10^\circ} {2} \right)\approx 2.0102\text{ s}.</math>
The linear approximation gives

<math display="block">2\pi \sqrt{\frac{1\text{ m}}{g}} \approx 2.0064\text{ s}.</math>

The difference between the two values, less than 0.2%, is on the same order of magnitude as the maximum variation of {{mvar|g}} with geographical location.

From here there are many ways to proceed to calculate the elliptic integral.

=== Legendre polynomial solution for the elliptic integral ===
Given {{EquationNote|Eq. 3}} and the [[Legendre polynomial]] solution for the elliptic integral:
<math display="block">K(k) =\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{(2n-1)!!}{(2n)!!}k^{n}\right)^{2}</math>
where {{math|''n''!!}} denotes the [[double factorial]], an exact solution to the period of a simple pendulum is:
<math display="block">\begin{alignat}{2}
T & = 2\pi \sqrt\frac \ell g \left( 1+ \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^2 \sin^2 \frac{\theta_0}{2} + \left( \frac{1 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 4} \right)^2 \sin^4 \frac{\theta_0}{2} + \left( \frac {1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6} \right)^2 \sin^6 \frac{\theta_0}{2} + \cdots \right) \\
 & = 2\pi \sqrt\frac\ell g \cdot \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left( \left ( \frac{(2n)!}{( 2^n \cdot n! )^2} \right )^2 \cdot \sin^{2 n}\frac{\theta_0}{2} \right).\end{alignat}</math>

Figure 4 shows the relative errors using the power series. {{math|''T''<sub>0</sub>}} is the linear approximation, and {{math|''T''<sub>2</sub>}} to {{math|''T''<sub>10</sub>}} include respectively the terms up to the 2nd to the 10th powers.

=== Power series solution for the elliptic integral ===
Another formulation of the above solution can be found if the following Maclaurin series:
<math display="block">\sin \frac{\theta_0} 2 =\frac12\theta_0 - \frac{1}{48}\theta_0^3 + \frac{1}{3\,840}\theta_0^5 - \frac{1}{645\,120}\theta_0^7 + \cdots.</math>
is used in the Legendre polynomial solution above.
The resulting power series is:<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Nelson | first1 = Robert | first2 = M. G. | last2 = Olsson | title = The pendulum — Rich physics from a simple system | journal = American Journal of Physics | volume = 54 | issue = 2 | pages = 112–121 | date = February 1986 <!-- | url = http://ajp.aapt.org/resource/1/ajpias/v54/i2/p112_s1 dead link --> <!-- | access-date = 2012-04-30| bibcode =1986AmJPh..54..112N --> | doi = 10.1119/1.14703 | bibcode = 1986AmJPh..54..112N | s2cid = 121907349 }}</ref>

<math display="block">T = 2\pi \sqrt\frac\ell g \left( 1+ \frac{1}{16}\theta_0^2 + \frac{11}{3\,072}\theta_0^4 + \frac{173}{737\,280}\theta_0^6 + \frac{22\,931}{1\,321\,205\,760}\theta_0^8 + \frac{1\,319\,183}{951\,268\,147\,200}\theta_0^{10} + \frac{233\,526\,463}{2\,009\,078\,326\,886\,400}\theta_0^{12} + \cdots \right),</math>
more fractions available in the [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]] with {{OEIS2C|A223067}} having the numerators and {{OEIS2C|A223068}} having the denominators.

=== Arithmetic-geometric mean solution for elliptic integral ===
Given {{EquationNote|Eq. 3}} and the [[arithmetic–geometric mean]] solution of the elliptic integral:
<math display="block">K(k) = \frac {\pi}{2 M(1-k,1+k)},</math>
where {{math|''M''(''x'',''y'')}} is the arithmetic-geometric mean of {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}}.

This yields an alternative and faster-converging formula for the period:<ref name=Carvalhaes>{{Citation |title=Approximations for the period of the simple pendulum based on the arithmetic-geometric mean |url=https://suppes-corpus.stanford.edu/sites/g/files/sbiybj7316/f/approximations_for_the_period_of_the_simple_pendulum_based_on_the_arithmetic-geometric_mean_431.pdf |first1=Claudio G. |last1=Carvalhaes |first2=Patrick |last2=Suppes |journal=[[American Journal of Physics|Am. J. Phys.]] |issn=0002-9505 |volume=76 |issue=12͒ |date=December 2008 |pages=1150–1154 |doi=10.1119/1.2968864 |access-date=2013-12-14| bibcode=2008AmJPh..76.1150C }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1-link=Jonathan Borwein |first1=J.M. |last1=Borwein| author2-link=Peter Borwein |first2=P.B. |last2=Borwein |title=Pi and the AGM |publisher=Wiley |place=New York |year=1987 |isbn=0-471-83138-7 |mr=0877728 |pages=1–15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |title=A New and Wonderful Pendulum Period Equation |first=Tom |last=Van Baak |journal=Horological Science Newsletter |date=November 2013 |volume=2013 |issue=5 |pages=22–30 |url=http://www.leapsecond.com/hsn2006/pendulum-period-agm.pdf}}</ref>
<math display="block">T = \frac{2\pi}{M\left(1, \cos\frac{\theta_0} 2 \right)} \sqrt\frac\ell g.</math>

The first iteration of this algorithm gives
<math display="block">T_1 = \frac{2T_0}{1 + \cos \frac{\theta_0}{2}}. </math>

This approximation has the relative error of less than 1% for angles up to 96.11 degrees.<ref name=Carvalhaes /> Since <math display="inline">\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\cos\left(\frac{\theta_0}{2}\right)\right) = \cos^2 \frac{\theta_0}{4},</math> the expression can be written more concisely as
<math display="block">T_1 = T_0 \sec^2 \frac{\theta_0}{4}.</math>

The second order expansion of <math>\sec^2(\theta_0/4)</math> reduces to <math display="inline">T \approx T_0 \left(1 + \frac{\theta_0^2}{16} \right).</math>

A second iteration of this algorithm gives
<math display="block">T_2 = \frac{4T_0}{1 + \cos \frac{\theta_0}{2} + 2\sqrt{\cos \frac{\theta_0}{2}}} = \frac{4T_0}{\left(1 + \sqrt{\cos \frac{\theta_0}{2}} \right)^2}. </math>

This second approximation has a relative error of less than 1% for angles up to 163.10 degrees.<ref name=Carvalhaes />

== Approximate formulae for the nonlinear pendulum period ==
Though the exact period <math>T</math> can be determined, for any finite amplitude <math>\theta_0 < \pi</math> rad, by evaluating the corresponding complete elliptic integral <math>K(k)</math>, where <math>k \equiv \sin(\theta_0/2)</math>, this is often avoided in applications because it is not possible to express this integral in a closed form in terms of elementary functions. This has made way for research on simple approximate formulae for the increase of the pendulum period with amplitude (useful in introductory physics labs, classical mechanics, electromagnetism, acoustics, electronics, [[superconductivity]], etc.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Lima|first=F. M. S.|date=2008-09-10|title=Simple 'log formulae' for pendulum motion valid for any amplitude |url=http://stacks.iop.org/0143-0807/29/i=5/a=021?key=crossref.78b07aabf445ee2e2934f76c20a9cff4|journal=European Journal of Physics|volume=29|issue=5|pages=1091–1098|doi=10.1088/0143-0807/29/5/021|s2cid=121743087 |issn=0143-0807|via=IoP journals|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The approximate formulae found by different authors can be classified as follows:

* ‘Not so large-angle’ formulae, i.e. those yielding good estimates for amplitudes below <math>\pi/2</math> rad (a natural limit for a bob on the end of a flexible string), though the deviation with respect to the exact period increases monotonically with amplitude, being unsuitable for amplitudes near to <math>\pi</math> rad. One of the simplest formulae found in literature is the following one by Lima (2006): <math display="inline">T \approx -\,T_0 \, \frac{\ln{a}}{1-a}</math>, where <math>a \equiv \cos{(\theta_0/2)}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lima|first1=F. M. S.|last2=Arun|first2=P.|date=October 2006|title=An accurate formula for the period of a simple pendulum oscillating beyond the small angle regime|journal=American Journal of Physics|volume=74|issue=10 | pages=892–895|doi=10.1119/1.2215616|issn=0002-9505|arxiv=physics/0510206| bibcode=2006AmJPh..74..892L|s2cid=36304104}}</ref>
* ‘Very large-angle’ formulae, i.e. those which approximate the exact period asymptotically for amplitudes near to <math>\pi</math>rad, with an error that increases monotonically for smaller amplitudes (i.e., unsuitable for small amplitudes). One of the better such formulae is that by Cromer, namely:<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cromer|first=Alan|date=February 1995 | title=Many oscillations of a rigid rod|journal=American Journal of Physics|volume=63|issue=2|pages=112–121 | doi=10.1119/1.17966|bibcode=1995AmJPh..63..112C|issn=0002-9505}}</ref> <math display="inline">T \approx \frac{2}{\pi}\,T_0\,\ln{(4/a)}</math>.

Of course, the increase of <math>T</math> with amplitude is more apparent when <math>\pi/2<\theta_0<\pi</math>, as has been observed in many experiments using either a rigid rod or a disc.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gil|first1=Salvador| last2=Legarreta| first2=Andrés E.|last3=Di Gregorio|first3=Daniel E.|date=September 2008|title=Measuring anharmonicity in a large amplitude pendulum | journal=American Journal of Physics|volume=76|issue=9|pages=843–847|doi=10.1119/1.2908184| bibcode=2008AmJPh..76..843G | issn=0002-9505}}</ref> As accurate timers and sensors are currently available even in introductory physics labs, the experimental errors found in ‘very large-angle’ experiments are already small enough for a comparison with the exact period, and a very good agreement between theory and experiments in which friction is negligible has been found. Since this activity has been encouraged by many instructors, a simple approximate formula for the pendulum period valid for all possible amplitudes, to which experimental data could be compared, was sought. In 2008, Lima derived a weighted-average formula with this characteristic:<ref name=":0" />
<math display="block">T \approx \frac{r\,a^2\,T_\text{Lima} +k^2\,T_\text{Cromer}}{r\,a^2+k^2},</math>
where <math>r = 7.17</math>, which presents a maximum error of only 0.6% (at <math>\theta_0 = 95^\circ</math>).

== Arbitrary-amplitude angular displacement ==
The [[Fourier series]] expansion of <math>\theta(t)</math> is given by<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lawden |first=Derek F. |title=Elliptic Functions and Applications|publisher=Springer-Verlag |year=1989 |isbn=0-387-96965-9|page=40}} Eq. 2.7.9: <math display=inline>-kk'\int\operatorname{sd}u\, \mathrm du=\arcsin (k\operatorname{cd}u)+C</math></ref><ref>{{dlmf|first1=W. P.|last1=Reinhardt|first2=P. L.|last2=Walker|id=22.11.E5|title=Jacobian Elliptic Functions}}</ref>

<math display=block>
\theta(t) = 8\sum_{n \geq 1\text{ odd}}\frac{(-1)^{\left\lfloor{n/2}\right\rfloor}}{n}\frac{q^{n/2}}{1+q^{n}}\cos(n\omega t)
</math>

where <math>q</math> is the [[Nome (mathematics)|elliptic nome]], <math>q=\exp\left({-\pi K\bigl(\sqrt{\textstyle 1-k^2}\bigr) \big/ K(k)}\right),</math> <math>k=\sin (\theta_0/2),</math> and <math>\omega=2\pi/T</math> the [[angular frequency]].

If one defines
<math display="block">\varepsilon=\frac12\cdot \frac{1-\sqrt{\cos(\theta_0/2)}}{1+\sqrt{\cos(\theta_0/2)}} </math>
<math>q</math> can be approximated using the expansion
<math display="block">q = \varepsilon + 2\varepsilon^5 + 15\varepsilon^{9} + 150\varepsilon^{13} + 1707\varepsilon^{17} + 20910\varepsilon^{21} + \cdots </math>
(see {{OEIS2C|A002103}}). Note that <math>\varepsilon < \tfrac 1 2</math> for <math>\theta_0<\pi</math>, thus the approximation is applicable even for large amplitudes.

Equivalently, the angle can be given in terms of the [[Jacobi elliptic functions|Jacobi elliptic function]] <math>\operatorname{cd}</math> with modulus <math>k</math><ref>{{cite web | url=https://medium.com/physicsfromscratch/a-complete-solution-to-the-non-linear-pendulum-9afda0b64926 | title=A Complete Solution to the Non-Linear Pendulum | date=4 December 2021 }}</ref>
<math display="block">\theta(t)=2\arcsin\left(k\operatorname{cd}\left(\sqrt{\frac{g}{\ell}}t;k\right)\right),\quad k=\sin\frac{\theta_0}{2}.</math>

For small <math>x</math>, <math>\sin x\approx x</math>, <math>\arcsin x\approx x</math> and <math>\operatorname{cd}(t;0)=\cos t</math>, so the solution is well-approximated by the solution given in [[Pendulum (mechanics)#Small-angle approximation]].

== Compound pendulum ==
A '''compound pendulum''' (or '''physical pendulum''') is one where the rod is not massless, and may have extended size; that is, an arbitrarily shaped [[rigid body]] swinging by a pivot <math>O</math>. In this case the pendulum's period depends on its [[moment of inertia]] <math>I_O</math> around the pivot point.

The equation of [[torque]] gives:
<math display="block">\tau = I \alpha</math>
where:
<math>\alpha</math> is the angular acceleration.
<math>\tau</math> is the torque

The torque is generated by gravity so:
<math>\tau = - m g r_\oplus \sin\theta</math>
where:
*<math>m</math> is the total mass of the rigid body (rod and bob)
*<math>r_\oplus</math> is the distance from the pivot point to the system's centre-of-mass
*<math>\theta</math> is the angle from the vertical

Hence, under the small-angle approximation, <math>\sin\theta\approx\theta</math> (or equivalently when <math>\theta_\mathrm{max}\ll 1</math>),
<math display="block">\alpha = \ddot{\theta} = \frac{mgr_\oplus}{I_O}\sin\theta \approx -\frac{mgr_\oplus}{I_O}\theta</math>
where <math>I_O</math> is the moment of inertia of the body about the pivot point <math>O</math>.

The expression for <math>\alpha</math> is of the same form as the conventional simple pendulum and gives a period of<ref name="Hyperphysics" />
<math display="block">T = 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{I_O}{mgr_\oplus}}</math>

And a frequency of
<math display="block">f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{mgr_\oplus}{I_O}}</math>

If the initial angle is taken into consideration (for large amplitudes), then the expression for <math>\alpha</math> becomes: 
<math display="block">\alpha = \ddot{\theta} = -\frac{mgr_\oplus}{I_O}\sin\theta</math>
and gives a period of: 
<math display="block">T = 4 \operatorname{K}\left(\sin^2\frac{\theta_\mathrm{max}}{2}\right) \sqrt{\frac{I_O}{mgr_\oplus}}</math>
where <math>\theta_\mathrm{max}</math> is the maximum angle of oscillation (with respect to the vertical) and <math>\operatorname{K}(k)</math> is the [[Elliptic integral#Complete elliptic integral of the first kind|complete elliptic integral of the first kind]].

An important concept is the '''equivalent length''', <math>\ell^\mathrm{eq}</math>, the length of a simple pendulums that has the same angular frequency <math>\omega_0</math> as the compound pendulum:
<math> {\omega_0}^2 = \frac{g}{\ell^\mathrm{eq}} := \frac{mgr_\oplus}{I_O} \implies \ell^\mathrm{eq} = \frac{I_O}{mr_\oplus} </math>

Consider the following cases:
* The simple pendulum is the special case where all the mass is located at the bob swinging at a distance <math>\ell</math> from the pivot. Thus, <math>r_\oplus=\ell</math> and <math>I_O=m\ell^2</math>, so the expression reduces to: <math>{\omega_0}^2 = \frac{mgr_\oplus}{I_O}=\frac{mg\ell}{m\ell^2}=\frac{g}{\ell}</math> . Notice <math>\ell^\mathrm{eq}=\ell</math>, as expected (the definition of equivalent length).
* A homogeneous rod of mass <math>m</math> and length <math>\ell</math> swinging from its end has <math>r_\oplus=\frac{1}{2}\ell</math> and <math>I_O=\frac{1}{3}m\ell^2</math>, so the expression reduces to: <math>{\omega_0}^2 = \frac{mgr_\oplus}{I_O}=\frac{mg\,\frac{1}{2}\ell}{\frac{1}{3}m\ell^2}=\frac{g}{\frac{2}{3}\ell}</math> . Notice <math>\ell^\mathrm{eq}=\frac{2}{3}\ell</math>, a homogeneous rod oscillates as if it were a simple pendulum of two-thirds its length.
* A heavy simple pendulum: combination of a homogeneous rod of mass <math>m_\mathrm{rod}</math> and length <math>\ell</math> swinging from its end, and a bob <math>m_\mathrm{bob}</math> at the other end. Then the system has a total mass of <math>m_\mathrm{bob}+m_\mathrm{rod}</math>, and the other parameters being <math>m r_\oplus=m_\mathrm{bob}\ell+m_\mathrm{rod}\frac{\ell}{2}</math> (by definition of centre-of-mass) and <math>I_O=m_\mathrm{bob}\ell^2+\frac{1}{3}m_\mathrm{rod}\ell^2</math>, so the expression reduces to: 
<math>{\omega_0}^2 = \frac{mgr_\oplus}{I_O}=\frac{\left(m_\mathrm{bob}\ell+m_\mathrm{rod}\frac{\ell}{2}\right)g}{m_\mathrm{bob}\ell^2+\frac{1}{3}m_\mathrm{rod}\ell^2} = \frac{g}{\ell} \frac{m_\mathrm{bob}+\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{2}}{m_\mathrm{bob}+\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{3}} = \frac{g}{\ell} \frac{1+\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{2m_\mathrm{bob}}}{1+\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{3m_\mathrm{bob}}} </math>
Where <math>\ell^\mathrm{eq} = \ell \frac{1+\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{3m_\mathrm{bob}}} {1+\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{2m_\mathrm{bob}}} </math>. Notice these formulae can be particularized into the two previous cases studied before just by considering the mass of the rod or the bob to be zero respectively. Also notice that the formula does not depend on both the mass of the bob and the rod, but actually on their ratio, <math>\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{m_\mathrm{bob}}</math>.  An approximation can be made for <math>\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{m_\mathrm{bob}}\ll 1</math>:

<math>{\omega_0}^2 \approx \frac{g}{\ell} \left( 1+\frac{1}{6}\frac{m_\mathrm{rod}}{m_\mathrm{bob}}+\cdots\right)</math>

Notice how similar it is to the angular frequency in a [[Effective_mass_(spring–mass_system)|spring-mass system with effective mass]].

== Damped, driven pendulum ==
The above discussion focuses on a pendulum bob only acted upon by the force of gravity. Suppose a damping force, e.g. air resistance, as well as a sinusoidal driving force acts on the body. This system is a damped, driven [[Harmonic oscillator|oscillator]], and is [[Chaos theory|chaotic]].

Equation (1) can be written as

<math display="block">ml^2 \frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2}  = -mgl \sin \theta</math>

(see the [[#Simple gravity pendulum|Torque derivation of Equation (1)]] above).

A damping term and forcing term can be added to the right hand side to get

<math display="block">ml^2 \frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2} = -mgl\sin \theta - b\frac{d\theta}{dt} + a\cos(\Omega t)</math>

where the damping is assumed to be directly proportional to the angular velocity (this is true for low-speed air resistance, see also [[Drag (physics)]]). <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are constants defining the amplitude of forcing and the degree of damping respectively. <math display="inline">\Omega</math> is the angular frequency of the driving oscillations.

Dividing through by <math display="inline">ml^2</math>:

<math display="block">\frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2} + \frac{b}{ml^2}\frac{d\theta}{dt} + \frac{g}{l}{\sin \theta} - \frac{a}{ml^2}\cos (\Omega t) = 0.</math>

For a physical pendulum:

<math display="block">\frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2} + \frac{b}{I}\frac{d\theta}{dt} + \frac{mgr_\oplus}{I}{\sin \theta} - \frac{a}{I}\cos (\Omega t) = 0.</math>

This equation exhibits [[Chaos theory|chaotic behaviour]]. The exact motion of this pendulum can only be found numerically and is highly dependent on initial conditions, e.g. the initial velocity and the starting amplitude. However, the small angle approximation outlined above can still be used under the required conditions to give an approximate analytical solution.

== Physical interpretation of the imaginary period ==
The [[Jacobi's elliptic functions|Jacobian elliptic function]] that expresses the position of a pendulum as a function of time is a [[doubly periodic function]] with a [[real number|real]] period and an [[imaginary number|imaginary]] period. The real period is, of course, the time it takes the pendulum to go through one full cycle. [[Paul Appell]] pointed out a physical interpretation of the imaginary period:<ref>{{cite journal|first=Paul |last=Appell |title=Sur une interprétation des valeurs imaginaires du temps en Mécanique |trans-title=On an interpretation of imaginary time values in mechanics |journal=[[Comptes Rendus Hebdomadaires des Séances de l'Académie des Sciences]] |volume=87 |issue=1 |date=July 1878}}</ref> if {{math|''θ''<sub>0</sub>}} is the maximum angle of one pendulum and {{math|180° − ''θ''<sub>0</sub>}} is the maximum angle of another, then the real period of each is the magnitude of the imaginary period of the other.

== Coupled pendula ==
[[File:Coupled pendulums.svg|thumb|415x415px|Two identical simple pendulums coupled via a spring connecting the bobs.]]
'''Coupled pendulums''' can affect each other's motion, either through a direction connection (such as a spring connecting the bobs) or through motions in a supporting structure (such as a tabletop). The equations of motion for two identical simple pendulums coupled by a spring connecting the bobs can be obtained using [[Lagrangian mechanics]].

The kinetic energy of the system is:
<math display="block">E_\text{K}=\frac{1}{2}mL^2\left(\dot\theta_1^2+\dot\theta_2^2\right)</math>
where <math>m</math> is the mass of the bobs, <math>L</math> is the length of the strings, and <math>\theta_1</math>, <math>\theta_2</math> are the angular displacements of the two bobs from equilibrium.

The potential energy of the system is:
<math display="block">E_\text{p}=mgL(2-\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)+\frac{1}{2}kL^2(\theta_2-\theta_1)^2</math>

where <math>g</math> is the [[gravitational acceleration]], and <math>k</math> is the [[Hooke's law|spring constant]]. The displacement <math>L(\theta_2-\theta_1)</math> of the spring from its equilibrium position assumes the [[Small-angle approximation|small angle approximation]].

The Lagrangian is then
<math display="block">\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}mL^2\left(\dot\theta_1^2+\dot\theta_2^2\right)-mgL(2-\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)-\frac{1}{2} k L^2(\theta_2-\theta_1)^2</math>
which leads to the following set of coupled differential equations:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\ddot\theta_1+\frac{g}{L}\sin\theta_1+\frac{k}{m}(\theta_1-\theta_2)&=0 \\
\ddot\theta_2+\frac{g}{L}\sin\theta_2-\frac{k}{m}(\theta_1-\theta_2)&=0
\end{align}</math>

Adding and subtracting these two equations in turn, and applying the small angle approximation, gives two [[Harmonic oscillator#Simple harmonic oscillator|harmonic oscillator]] equations in the variables <math>\theta_1+\theta_2</math> and <math>\theta_1-\theta_2</math>:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\ddot\theta_1+\ddot\theta_2+\frac{g}{L}(\theta_1+\theta_2)&=0 \\
\ddot\theta_1-\ddot\theta_2+\left(\frac{g}{L}+2\frac{k}{m}\right)(\theta_1-\theta_2)&=0
\end{align}</math>
with the corresponding solutions
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\theta_1+\theta_2&=A\cos(\omega_1t+\alpha) \\
\theta_1-\theta_2&=B\cos(\omega_2t+\beta)
\end{align}</math>
where
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\omega_1&=\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}} \\
\omega_2&=\sqrt{\frac{g}{L}+2\frac{k}{m}}
\end{align}</math>

and <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>\alpha</math>, <math>\beta</math> are [[Constant of integration|constants of integration]].

Expressing the solutions in terms of <math>\theta_1</math> and <math>\theta_2</math> alone:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\theta_1&=\frac{1}{2}A\cos(\omega_1t+\alpha)+\frac{1}{2}B\cos(\omega_2t+\beta) \\
\theta_2&=\frac{1}{2}A\cos(\omega_1t+\alpha)-\frac{1}{2}B\cos(\omega_2t+\beta)
\end{align}</math>

If the bobs are not given an initial push, then the condition <math>\dot\theta_1(0)=\dot\theta_2(0)=0</math> requires <math>\alpha=\beta=0</math>, which gives (after some rearranging):
<math display="block">\begin{align}
A&=\theta_1(0)+\theta_2(0)\\
B&=\theta_1(0)-\theta_2(0)
\end{align}</math>
